meeting_header: Date: 2026-07-18 | Time: 14:00 UTC | Duration: 45m | Attendees: Jordan Park (Redwood AE), Sofia Martinez (Redwood SE), Liam O'Connor (Redwood CSM), Priya Nair (Argentum Head of ML), Tom Ellis (Argentum Platform Eng), Amir Haddad (Argentum CTO), Rosa Kim (Argentum Data Privacy)
transcript:
[00:00] Jordan Park: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call?
[00:07] Priya Nair: Hi, Priya here.
[00:09] Tom Ellis: Tom - platform.
[00:11] Amir Haddad: Amir, hi.
[00:13] Jordan Park: Great. We got 45 minutes — main goals: review last week’s bench numbers, talk caching and batching tradeoffs, and align next steps. Sofia, quick recap?
[00:25] Sofia Martinez: Yeah, thanks. So we ran the mixed workload bench you gave us last week, um, two configs: hosted gpt-like profile on Redwood hosted and a dedicated 2xA100 instance on Redwood Dedicated. Short version: dedicated is about 2.6x tokens/sec for the 512-token prompts at median but cost per token shifts depending on utilization. There was also a big delta from the KV cache hit rate, which on your app trace was around 18% average, we saw simulated savings up to 35% with a modest prefix cache TTL.
[00:55] Priya Nair: Wait 35%? That seems high — were you caching the full user history or only static system prompts?
[01:03] Sofia Martinez: Mostly static system prompts and repeated few-shot contexts. We modeled a 30-second TTL for conversational sessions and aggressive prefix caching for identical user intents. If you have very dynamic user-generated content the effective hit rate drops.
[01:18] Tom Ellis: Our traffic pattern is bursty — morning spike then idle mid-day. How does that affect tokens/sec/$?
[01:25] Sofia Martinez: Good question. On dedicated we assume reserved capacity cost amortized. With your bursty profile, tokens/sec/$ improves with higher steady utilization. But with spikes under hosted, Redwood's burst capacity and autoscaling can keep latency SLOs but costs more per token for the burst minutes. We put together a simple metric: tokens per dollar per minute window. At 70% avg util dedicated was best; at <25% hosted is cheaper unless you negotiate reserved pool.
[01:50] Amir Haddad: Can you show numbers?
[01:52] Sofia Martinez: Sure. From the run: hosted (baseline model) — median latency 120ms, tokens/sec about 580 for the batch size we used, cost assumption $0.014/token-equivalent — giving ~41k tokens/$/hourish? (note: rough). Dedicated 2xA100 — tokens/sec ~1500, median latency 90ms, but amortized cost changes: if your steady utilization is low token unit-cost becomes higher because you're paying for reserved nodes even when idle.
[02:28] Priya Nair: Are these numbers including quantized model variants?
[02:31] Sofia Martinez: We tested both FP16 and 4-bit quantized variants. Quant improves throughput 10–20% and reduces memory pressure; however there's a small quality regression on certain prompts — score drop of ~0.6% on your eval set. So it's a tradeoff.
[02:48] Jordan Park: Also, note that caching + quantization stacks — if you can cache early prefixes you reduce tokens generated and that can make quantization more attractive since fewer tokens are generated overall.
[02:59] Tom Ellis: Latency tail for us matters a lot — checkout flow times need 200ms p95. How did tail behave?
[03:07] Sofia Martinez: P95 for dedicated was 220ms in our initial runs because of serialization spikes; after enabling continuous micro-batching and pre-warmed KV cache the p95 dropped to 160ms. On hosted p95 stayed around 300ms during spikes. So if tail matters, dedicated with warmers and prewarmed instances wins.
[03:30] Priya Nair: What about batching? We thought batching would always help tokens/sec but we worry about added latency.
[03:36] Sofia Martinez: Right — batching improves aggregate throughput but can hurt single-request latency. We simulated three policies: 1) conservative batching (max batch 4, wait 5ms) gave moderate throughput gains and negligible added latency; 2) aggressive batching (max 16, wait 20ms) gave ~40% throughput but increased p95 by ~30ms; 3) dynamic latency-first batching (adaptive wait based on queue) gave best balance in steady-state but is sensitive during spikes. For checkout flows we recommended latency-first with small batch caps and aggressive warmup. For background tasks, aggressive batching.
[04:15] Amir Haddad: The team cares about tokens/sec per dollar. Can you summarize the tokens/sec/$ delta across typical windows?
[04:21] Sofia Martinez: Yep. Short summary (very rough): under realistic mix and current cloud pricing: hosted bursts: ~30–50k tokens per dollar depending on model size; dedicated at 70% util: ~120–160k tokens per dollar; dedicated at 20% util: ~35–55k tokens per dollar because of idle amortization. Cache hit rates of 20–35% translate to 15–35% reduction in token bill.
[04:49] Priya Nair: OK that matches intuition. Any suggestions for immediate wins?
[04:53] Sofia Martinez: Three quick wins: 1) enable prefix KV caching for repeated system prompts (easy config), 2) set small batching caps for latency-critical endpoints and aggressive for background tasks, 3) evaluate quantized flavor on a small eval set and monitor hallucination/quality regressions via Redwood Console eval dashboards.
[05:12] Tom Ellis: On caching - what about memory and eviction? Is there an operator cost?
[05:18] Sofia Martinez: Memory footprint grows with cached prefix count. We typically provision a small LRU cache on the inference nodes; operators set a TTL and size cap. For your traffic the recommended setting was 40MB per node for the session-level prefix cache; eviction is automatic, and Redwood Console exposes hit/miss metrics.
[05:33] Priya Nair: Are there any compliance or PII concerns when caching? Rosa, want to chime in?
[05:38] Rosa Kim: Yes, if caching user PII we need to mask and also consider retention windows. We prefer caching only system prompts and pseudonymized context. Also need audit logs for access — does Redwood console provide that?
[05:48] Liam O'Connor: Redwood Console includes token-level cost/latency breakdown and per-route logs; for Private deployments we map logs to your KMS and the audit trail remains in your VPC. We can share the SOC2 artifact as well.
[06:05] Priya Nair: Good. Back to economics — Jordan, can you sketch a hybrid recommendation?
[06:10] Jordan Park: Sure. Hybrid recommended for Argentum: reserve a small Dedicated pool sized for baseline 50% of expected steady QPS, leave rest on hosted with autoscale for spikes. Use prefix caching to cut token volume, small-batch latency-first policy for checkout endpoints, aggressive batching for background pipelines, and a 4-bit quantized variant for background where quality tolerance is higher.
[06:34] Amir Haddad: How does fallback work if dedicated is saturated?
[06:37] Sofia Martinez: Smart routing: we set a routing policy to fall back to hosted identical model family; you'd see slightly higher latency and cost per-token for those requests. We also recommended a canary capacity for autoscale to warm nodes.
[06:50] Tom Ellis: Any hidden costs we missed — egress, S3, KV storage?
[06:53] Sofia Martinez: Egress and storage are normal infra costs; caching reduces generated tokens more than it reduces egress. There is small storage for cached prefix metadata, negligible relative to tokens.
[07:05] Priya Nair: One more thing on quality — how did quantized runs affect our intent-class accuracy?
[07:10] Sofia Martinez: On your eval set, top-intent accuracy dropped from 92.1% to 91.5% on 4-bit for certain edge prompts. We flagged 6 prompts where completion altered entities. We can flag those for rule-based post-processing.
[07:25] Jordan Park: We also noticed some transcription artifacts in your logs — a couple of prompt templates had templating tokens that confused prefix hashing. Fixing templates and normalizing often boosts cache hit rate by 5–8%.
[07:38] Tom Ellis: That's interesting — we can send the template repo.
[07:40] Priya Nair: Yes, we'll share.
[07:43] Sofia Martinez: Great — also, we want to run a follow-up bench focusing on real-world tail latency under spotty network. That will help size pre-warmed instances.
[07:53] Amir Haddad: Sounds good.
[07:55] Jordan Park: Any blockers on Redwood side?
[07:58] Sofia Martinez: None — just coordination on dataset and permission to run the dedicated bench with sample traffic.
[08:05] Priya Nair: We'll grant access to a masked traffic dump.
[08:09] Rosa Kim: We'll redact PII prior. We'll also want to confirm KMS integration before moving to Private.
[08:16] Liam O'Connor: We'll loop in our security eng for that scoping call.
[08:20] Jordan Park: OK wrap up — quick recap of next steps and owners, then we'll close.
[08:25] Sofia Martinez: Recap: bench run on 2xA100 (Sofia), pricing sheet update (Jordan), prompt corpus (Priya), SOC2 scoping (Rosa + Liam).
[08:36] Priya Nair: All good. Thanks.
[08:38] Jordan Park: Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites.
[08:41] [meeting ends]

Summary:
- Dedicated improves tokens/sec substantially at higher utilization; amortization means low-utilization teams may prefer hosted or smaller reserved pools.
- Prefix/KV caching shown to reduce token generation by up to ~35% in modeled scenarios; templating normalization can add additional hit rate.
- Batching gains vs latency tradeoffs: use latency-first small batches for interactive flows, aggressive batching for background.
- Quantization gives throughput gains but small quality regressions on edge prompts; recommended for background jobs first.

Topics covered:
- Throughput (tokens/sec) vs cost (tokens/$) across hosted and dedicated
- Cache hit modelling and TTL recommendations
- Batching policies and latency impact (p95/p99)
- Quantization tradeoffs and eval impact
- Security/compliance and audit log mapping for Private
